newsitem.title: USA: Ex-surgeon general says tobacco complaints caused his firing.
newsitem.headline: Ex-surgeon general says tobacco complaints caused his firing.

text.p: The first U.S. surgeon general to propose secondhand-smoking curbs testified on Thursday he was fired 25 years ago after President Nixon's government was peppered with complaints from RJ Reynolds Tobacco Co.'s top executive about his anti-tobacco policies.

Jesse Steinfeld, America's top public health official from 1969 to early 1973, testified during a trial in which a class representing 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants is suing U.S. cigarette companies over secondhand smoke. He said that RJ Reynolds President David Peoples wrote repeatedly to his boss during 1972 to complain about his anti-tobacco activism and his 1971 proposal to curb smoking in public places on fears non-smokers were being hurt by secondhand smoke.
"Did you leave the office of Surgeon General before your term?" plaintiffs attorney Stanley Rosenblatt asked Steinfeld. "Were you fired?"
"That depends on your interpretation," Steinfeld said.

The trial judge did not allow questions about why Steinfeld's resignation was requested, but Steinfeld testified that Peoples had complained in a series of letters to Elliott Richardson, then Steinfeld's superior as U.S. Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare, about his anti-smoking initiatives, such as banning cigarette use in some government buildings.

Steinfeld, an academic physician, was named to a four-year term as surgeon general in late 1969 and expected to serve through 1973 or later. But he was asked for his resignation the day after Nixon's relection and left the government in January 1973.

He told reporters outside the courtroom that the Nixon White House was anxious about possible fallout from his resignation and asked him repeatedly to rewrite his resignation letter and to accept a manufactured motivation for his departure.
Scores of other government officials were also asked for resignations after the 1972 election as part of a Nixon campaign to shake up the federal bureaucracy, Steinfeld said.

Steinfeld told reporters that Peoples had also written to Nixon in October 1972 and reminded him in the letter of a chat the two had during a campaign fundraising event in which Nixon promised to drop Steinfeld as surgeon general.

Steinfeld said he was asked by Richardson to draft a response to the Peoples letter to Nixon and that Richardson, who had consistently defended him against the Reynolds complaints, passed on a response to the White House.

The Peoples letter is missing. Rival lawyers said Steinfeld was unable to locate his own copy of the Reynolds' official's letter, a search of Nixon's archives had proven fruitless and Reynolds was unable to find a copy of the letter.

Agreeing with lawyers defending the tobacco companies, Judge Robert Kaye of Dade County Court barred testimony about the Peoples letter to Nixon. Kaye said the letter's existence could not be sufficiently proven.
"This is total hearsay ... hearsay upon hearsay," said Hugh Whiting, an attorney for Reynolds, urging Kaye to forbid testimony on the missing letter.

Rosenblatt and his co-attorney and wife, Susan Rosenblatt, allege that the seven tobacco companies and two trade groups in the trial conspired for decades to blunt research and warnings about the health risks of smoking and secondhand smoke and sold products they knew were harmful.

The tobacco companies, yet to present their case, deny the conspiracy charges and say the incidence of lung cancer, emphysema and other tobacco-related disorders among the flight attendants was no higher than that of other people.
The flight attendants, all non-smokers, claim that passengers smoking aboard U.S. airlines before 1988 caused their injuries and are seeking $5 billion or more in damages in the class-action suit.
